title: 2026-04-01-adaptive-prefetch-and-streaming-batching-demo-with-galileo-med.json
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran an Optimize console demo focused on adaptive prefetch, streaming-aware batching, and prefix/KV cache recommendations for GalileoMed's clinical summarization workload. Conversation covered current architecture, cost targets, latency SLOs, suggested config knobs, and next steps to run a sandboxed savings sim. Several security and deployment constraints (PHI, VPC requirement) were raised and noted for follow-up.
next_steps: Redwood to share tailored Optimize playbook and cost simulation spreadsheet (Maya) - target Tue 2026-04-06
Galileo to provision short-lived test dataset and provide sample API traffic shape (Samir) - target Fri 2026-04-09
Schedule sandbox run for adaptive-prefetch with sample prompts (Ethan + Noah) - target week of 2026-04-13
action_items: Maya Patel: send Optimize playbook + cost workbook - due 2026-04-06
Samir Khatri: upload anonymized 48h traffic trace to shared bucket - due 2026-04-09
Ethan Cole: prepare sandbox config (streaming + adaptive-batching) and test suite - due 2026-04-12
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, really appreciate it. We're gonna walk through an Optimize console demo focusing on adaptive prefetch and streaming-aware batching. Quick intros?
[00:09] Dr. Lena (GalileoMed): Hi I'm Lena, head of ML at GalileoMed, we focus on clinical note summarization and triage.
[00:13] Samir (GalileoMed): Samir, infra lead, I'll be owning the test data and VPC setup.
[00:18] Priya (GalileoMed): Priya here, CTO. Quick on time but excited to see cost numbers.
[00:22] Ethan (Redwood SE): Ethan, solutions engineer, I'll dig into configs and run the sandbox with you.
[00:27] Maya: Great, quick agenda — 1) run through your current stack and constraints, 2) show Optimize recommended knobs (batching, prefix/KV), 3) run a short cost sim + Q&A, 4) agree next steps.
[00:38] Noah (GalileoMed): Sounds good.
[00:40] Maya: Samir, could you remind us of the current traffic profile? latency targets?
[00:44] Samir: Sure. Right now production is about 12k daily requests, peak concurrency ~40 concurrent streams for the summarizer. Latency SLO for interactive docs is 600ms p95, for batch nightly we allow longer.
[00:57] Ethan: Nice, so interactive target <600 ms p95. Are you streaming partial tokens to UI or waiting for full response?
[01:04] Dr. Lena: Streaming — users see partial summary as it's generated, that's important for triage.
[01:09] Ethan: OK that constrains batch size because streaming tends to favor smaller per-request tokens to keep tail low.
[01:15] Maya: Also curious about session reuse — do you maintain user conversation state or a one-shot summarization?
[01:21] Noah: It's mostly single-doc summarization with a short context of previous clinical notes (~1-3 prior entries). So we get some prefix reuse across calls from same patient.
[01:29] Ethan: That's great signal for prefix/KV caching; a lookahead/prefetch strategy could capture repeated initial context keys and save cost.
[01:35] Maya: Alright moving into the console demo — I'm going to share the Optimize playbook. (screen share)
[01:41] Maya: Top of the playbook is a recommended profile we generated from your sample traces — I ran a quick ingest before the call based on the 24-hour sample you uploaded last week.
[01:50] Priya: Wait, we uploaded a small sample — was that used to precompute recommendations?
[01:55] Ethan: Correct, Maya's team used the sample to fit a few parameters: token length distribution, prefix repetition ratio, and concurrency peaks. The model in the playbook assumes a mix of short summaries (~128 tokens) and long ones (~512), and a 22% prefix hit rate in the first 2 tokens.
[02:12] Dr. Lena: 22% seems high? I thought reuse was lower.
[02:16] Maya: The 22% refers to exact token-prefix reuse for the first 2–8 tokens across sessions, which in your logs happens for templated headers and encounter meta. Not full doc reuse.
[02:27] Samir: Ok makes sense.
[02:28] Maya: So recommendation #1 — enable prefix cache with a TTL of 10 minutes for session affinity and set lookup parallelism to 2. This reduces prefix compute for repeated record headers.
[02:39] Ethan: For streaming, we suggest adaptive batching: start with small batching window (8–12ms) at low concurrency and grow to 25–40ms when concurrency spikes. That captures micro-batching without violating p95.
[02:51] Maya: On the console you can simulate different batch windows — I'm going to run a quick savings sim using your profile (clicks).
[02:58] Maya: Running scenario A: prefix cache enabled TTL 10m, adaptive batch ramp 8-30ms, quantization profile FP16. Estimated token cost delta vs baseline is -37% and expected p95 impact ~+40ms.
[03:11] Priya: Wait 40ms increase in p95 is acceptable — that keeps us under 600ms?
[03:15] Ethan: Based on your baseline p95 around 540ms, adding 40ms still keeps you under 600ms, yes. But that assumes the prefix hit distribution is consistent; we'll validate in sandbox.
[03:25] Dr. Lena: How confident are you in the hit-rate assumption — if prefix reuse drops to 5% will we still see savings?
[03:30] Maya: Good question — scenario B in the playbook simulates a low-hit case. With 5% prefix hit and same batching policy savings drop to around -12% and p95 impact is negligible. So benefits scale with cache hit rate.
[03:42] Samir: What about KV cache memory pressure on the dedicated nodes? We're running dedicated GPUs for inference.
[03:47] Ethan: KV cache for prefix lookups stores compressed key vectors and is memory-efficient; we recommend bounding per-node KV size with eviction LRU and a per-tenant cap. Console shows recommended cap of 16GB per-shard for your workload which keeps miss penalty under 10ms.
[03:59] Maya: Also note the runtime supports hybrid routing — you can keep interactive on dedicated pool and offload heavy nightly jobs to hosted spot capacity to save costs.
[04:09] Priya: We absolutely need VPC for PHI. How does the private deployment change these recommendations?
[04:15] Ethan: The recommendations hold; on Private the KV index still runs locally in your VPC. The only difference is network egress and control-plane interactions — we can disable outbound telemetry if needed. Security docs link is in the deck.
[04:27] Dr. Lena: Show us the trade-off matrix again — I want to see how batch window size, concurrency, and cache TTL interact.
[04:33] Maya: (switches tabs) Here's a cost-heatmap: x-axis batch window 5–50ms, y-axis prefix TTL 1m–30m. Colors show delta in tokens-per-dollar. You can see a ridge where TTL 8–12m and batch 20–30ms give highest savings for your profile.
[04:50] Noah: Is that because longer TTL yields more reuse but also more stale keys?
[04:54] Ethan: Exactly — too long TTL increases cache churn and memory pressure; too short TTL misses reuse opportunities. For templates like yours, 8–12m is sweet.
[05:01] Samir: Any guidance on lookahead/prefetch aggressiveness? Should we prefetch the KV for the top-K likely continuations?
[05:07] Maya: We recommend a conservative prefetch of top-2 continuations per session for streaming, which reduces burst decoding cost without bloating I/O. More aggressive prefetch helps only if you have high repeatability of user prompts.
[05:17] Dr. Lena: Can you briefly show what the console will push to our engineers — configs and a simulated run?
[05:22] Ethan: Sure. (shares sandbox YAML) The sandbox config toggles: batch_window_ms: 20, adaptive_ramp: true, prefix_cache: enabled, prefix_ttl: 600, kv_shard_limit_gb: 16, prefetch_k: 2, fallback_model: small-variant.
[05:36] Maya: And here's the cost workbook breakdown — tokens, wall-clock compute, amortized KV maintenance, and per-request routing surcharge. For your 12k daily workload this config projects monthly hosting cost ~$9.2k vs baseline ~$14.6k — about 37% savings as earlier stated.
[05:53] Priya: Those numbers look promising. Is that using FP16 quantization across the model?
[05:58] Ethan: Yes FP16 for the generator and int8 for embedding pipeline where safe. We include a quality delta column — predicted ROUGE drop <0.5 for clinical notes in our internal eval on similar models, but we'll want your in-domain eval to confirm.
[06:12] Samir: Regarding rollouts, can we do canary at 5% traffic and auto-fallback if error rate or latency spikes?
[06:18] Maya: Absolutely. Console supports canary + automatic fallback to baseline model or to hosted variant if latency breach detected. We'll include recommended thresholds in the playbook.
[06:28] Dr. Lena: A few quick security questions: audit logs for token-level usage, KMS integration for keys, and proof of SOC2 coverage?
[06:36] Ethan: We have audit logs per-request, and Redwood Private integrates with your KMS (AWS KMS/HSM). We provide SOC2 Type II attestation — I'll attach the latest cert.
[06:46] Maya: (pulls up checklist) I'll paste the security artifacts link in the follow-up.
[06:50] Noah: On the model side — we want to compare outputs before/after quantization. Can the sandbox run A/B on identical prompts?
[06:56] Ethan: Yes, sandbox runner does paired A/B with side-by-side outputs and an automatic diff for key metrics (ROUGE, hallucination indicators). We'll wire that to your evaluation set.
[07:06] Dr. Lena: One thing we worry about is prompt injection and redaction of PHI in outputs, especially with streaming. Any mitigations?
[07:13] Ethan: We recommend prefix filtering and output post-processing hooks that run at the runtime edge — you can stash a policy model to validate tokens. Streaming complicates it but we can buffer the first N tokens until the content passes the policy check; tradeoff is added latency.
[07:28] Priya: Okay. Can you run one quick simulated scenario showing what happens when we hit a 3x concurrency spike?
[07:34] Maya: On it — switch to stress sim. (clicks) Scenario: concurrency spike to 120 (3x). With adaptive batching ramp and prefix cache, estimated cost per-request increases modestly but throughput holds. Without cache, compute spikes more and cost increases ~2.1x. With cache and fallback routing to hosted spot for background jobs, we keep tail latency under 950ms for interactive.
[07:56] Samir: 950ms is higher than we'd like, but acceptable for a failover mode.
[08:01] Ethan: We can tune routing policy to route only lower-importance sessions to hosted spot to protect critical interactive flows.
[08:07] Dr. Lena: Curious — you earlier mentioned a per-node KV cap of 16GB. If we go multi-shard for higher availability, how does that impact cost?
[08:15] Maya: Multi-shard increases memory footprint but reduces miss penalty and gives redundancy. Console will show incremental cost; for your workload going 3-way shard increases infra cost ~+8% but reduces tail latencies by ~12ms on average.
[08:29] Priya: Let's talk timeline — we want to pilot in prod in 6 weeks. Is that feasible?
[08:34] Ethan: Yes. Typical pilot path: sandbox (1–2 weeks), canary (1–2 weeks), expansion. Main dependencies: anonymized traces, VPC access and security review.
[08:45] Maya: Let me recap next steps: I'll send the playbook + cost workbook; Samir will upload 48h trace; Ethan will prepare sandbox config and run paired A/B with your eval set; we'll schedule the sandbox run week of April 13.
[08:58] Dr. Lena: Sounds good. One more question — competitor lock-in. If we move from hosted to dedicated to private, how portable are the configs?
[09:06] Ethan: Configs are portable — same Optimize policies, same batch/prefetch knobs. Only difference is network/keys. That portability is one of the platform design goals.
[09:15] Priya: Great. Anything else?
[09:17] Maya: Quick Q&A pause, any outstanding blockers?
[09:20] Samir: None on infra side besides the trace.
[09:22] Dr. Lena: No blockers.
[09:23] Noah: We'll take the playbook and get back on the sandbox schedule.
[09:26] Maya: Perfect, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and proposed calendar invites.
[09:31] End of recording.

Notes on transcript fidelity: occasional misattributions corrected where obvious; filler words and short crosstalk left in. There were a few micro-pauses and screen-share commentary omitted for brevity.
